accepted.question_text: For triangulations of the product polytope Δ_{n-1} × Δ_2 and of Δ_{n-1} × Δ_3, where a flip changes one triangulation into another and the flip graph has triangulations as vertices and flips as edges, is each of these two flip graphs Hamiltonian?

evidence.quote: Question: Are the flip graphs of triangulations of Δn−1 × Δ2 and Δn−1 × Δ3 Hamiltonian?

accepted.question_text: Let H_n be the subgraph of the associahedron graph G_n obtained from triangulations of a convex n-gon whose vertices are colored red and blue alternately, keeping only colorful triangulations with no monochromatic triangle. For odd n ≥ 7, does H_n contain a Hamilton path or a Hamilton cycle, and if so can such a structure be generated by an efficient algorithm?

evidence.quote: Question 1: Does Hn admit Hamilton paths or cycles for odd n ⩾ 7? If so, do these constructions translate into efficient algorithms?

accepted.question_text: If the coloring pattern on the vertices of an n-gon is allowed to be an arbitrary color sequence rather than the alternating red-blue pattern used to define H_n, what structural properties do the corresponding subgraphs of the associahedron have, and how do those properties change when more than two colors are allowed?

evidence.quote: Question 2: What about generalizing the coloring pattern of the n-gon from red, blue, red, blue, etc. to any other coloring sequence? This gives a huge family of interesting subgraphs of the associahedron. What are their properties? What happens with more than two colors?

accepted.question_text: How large can the chromatic number become for flip graphs of triangulations of a point set, for flip graphs of triangulations of a simple polygon, and for rotation graphs of elimination trees of a graph G, including natural structured families such as grids or trees?

evidence.quote:
Question: How large can the chromatic number be for the flip graph of triangulations of a point set P?
How large can the chromatic number be for the flip graph of triangulations of a simple polygon P?
How large can the chromatic number be for the rotation graph of elimination trees of a graph G? (binary search trees correspond to G = Pn)

accepted.question_text: A cycle-plus-triangles graph on 3n vertices is the union of a Hamiltonian cycle of length 3n and n vertex-disjoint triangles. What is the largest constant α for which one can efficiently find an independent set of size αn in every such graph, improving on the simple α ≥ 3/5 bound and moving closer to the open target α = 1?

evidence.quote: Question: What is the largest α for which we can efficiently find an αn-size independent set of a cycle-plus-triangles graph? As the graph is 4-regular, a simple algorithm yields α ⩾ 3/5, and α = 1 is the famous open question. Can we get α closer to 1?

accepted.question_text: In the communication model where Alice knows an n-city traveling salesperson instance and can compute an optimal tour, while Bob is restricted to polynomial-time computation and must reconstruct the optimal tour from Alice’s message, can Alice use at most 0.4999·n log2 n bits of advice, or even o(n log n) bits? What stronger upper bounds become possible if the distance function is metric or Euclidean?

evidence.quote: Question: Is there a strategy for Alice with 0.4999 · n log2 n or fewer bits of advice? More ambitiously, is there a solution with o(n log n) bits?
Can something stronger be shown if the distances are metric or euclidean?

accepted.question_text: For k ≤ 4, does there exist a pivot rule for the k-Opt local-search algorithm for the traveling salesperson problem such that, for every edge-weighted complete graph and every initial tour, repeated improving k-Opt steps are guaranteed to terminate in polynomial time? The question is especially interesting for k = 2 in the Euclidean setting.

evidence.quote: Question 1: For k ⩽ 4, is there a pivot rule such that k-Opt algorithm always terminates in polynomial time, for any pair of an edge-weighted complete graph G and an initial tour τ?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a value of k for which Euclidean TSP/k-Opt is PLS-complete?

evidence.quote: Question 2: Does there exist some k, for which Euclidean TSP/k-Opt is PLS-complete?

accepted.question_text: Are there nontrivial permutation classes C ⊆ S_n for which the restricted determinant-like and permanent-like sums det_C(A) = Σ_{π∈C} sgn(π) Π_i A_{i,π(i)} and per_C(A) = Σ_{π∈C} Π_i A_{i,π(i)} can be computed efficiently, and can such permutation classes be classified? The same question is also posed for general immanants.

evidence.quote: Question 1: Are there nontrivial permutation classes C ⊆ Sn such that detC(A) := Σ_{π∈C} sgn(π) Π_i Ai,π(i), and the similarly defined perC(A) can be computed efficiently? Can we even classify these classes?
These questions can also be asked for general immanants.

accepted.question_text: For 2-cut elimination trees on a tree G, where every rooted subtree T_v has boundary size at most 2 in the underlying graph, can the known 5n upper bound on rotation distance be improved?

evidence.quote: Question 1: 2-cut elimination trees are particularly interesting because they “locally” behave like binary trees. (Observe that each binary tree, i.e. elimination tree on a path, is 2-cut.) The (tight) rotation distance bound for binary trees is 2n − 6. Can the 5n bound for 2-cut trees be improved?

accepted.question_text: For k-cut elimination trees on a tree G, can the known upper bound on rotation distance be tightened from the current linear-in-k bound to O(n log k)?

evidence.quote: Question 2: The k-cut bound degenerates to Θ(n2) for k ≈ n, i.e., the general case. However, the rotation distance between elimination trees on trees is known to be only O(n log n) [2]. Can the k-cut bound be tightened to O(n log k)?

accepted.question_text: For k-cut elimination trees on general graphs of treewidth at most t, can the best known O(t·n log n) upper bound on rotation distance be improved to O(t·k·n), analogous to the O(k·n) bound known when the underlying graph is a tree?
accepted.context_brief: k-cut elimination trees on general graphs

evidence.quote: Question 3: What about k-cut trees on general graphs? A graph admits a k-cut tree if and only if it has treewidth at most k. The best known upper bound for treewidth-t graphs is O(t · n log n) [3]. For k-cut elimination trees, can we get O(t · k · n), analogous to the O(k · n) bound when G is a tree?

accepted.question_text: Given a matroid M on m elements presented by an independence oracle, can the diameter δ(M) of its base polytope be computed faster than the current polynomial-time reduction to matroid intersection, or can one prove a superlinear conditional lower bound? What better algorithms are possible in other representations such as graphic, realizable, lattice-path, or transversal matroids?

evidence.quote: Question: Can we do better in the oracle model? Is there a superlinear (conditional) lower bound? Can we design algorithms in another computation model, for matroids that are given in some specific forms, for instance graphic matroids (a graph), realizable matroids (a matrix), lattice path matroids [1], or, more generally, transversal matroids?

accepted.question_text: Are there classes of polytopes given in implicit or partially implicit form whose graph diameter can nonetheless be computed in polynomial time, and are there classes of polymatroids whose diameter can be computed efficiently?
accepted.context_brief: Diameter of implicit polytopes and polymatroids

evidence.quote: Question (vague): Are there other classes of polytopes, given in a more or less implicit form, whose diameter can be computed in polynomial time?
It would be interesting to know if there are classes of polymatroids whose diameter can be computed efficiently.

accepted.question_text: What is the computational complexity of computing the diameter of the bipartite perfect matching polytope, whose vertices are perfect matchings and whose edges correspond to flips of alternating cycles?
accepted.context_brief: Diameter of bipartite perfect matching polytope

evidence.quote: Question: What is the complexity of computing the diameter of the bipartite perfect matching polytope?

accepted.question_text: What is the smallest number K(n) such that every permutation of length n can be sorted into increasing order in at most K(n) rounds, where each round partitions the current sequence into disjoint consecutive blocks and reverses every block simultaneously?

evidence.quote: Question: What is the smallest number K(n) such that any input sequence of length n can be sorted in at most K(n) rounds? We may assume without loss of generality that the input is a permutation, i.e., a sequence containing each number from the set {1, 2, . . . , n} exactly once.

accepted.question_text: For any integer k and any skew shape S, is the number of transversal fillings of S that avoid decreasing k-chains always at most the number of transversal fillings that avoid increasing k-chains?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1. For any k and for any skew shape S, the number of transversals of S that avoid decreasing k-chains is smaller or equal to the number of transversals of S that avoid increasing k-chains.

accepted.question_text: If H_0 is the ordered graph shown in Figure 7, is the chromatic number of the class of ordered graphs that avoid H_0 as an ordered subgraph bounded by a constant?

evidence.quote: Question: Is the chromatic number of ordered graphs excluding H0 as an ordered subgraph bounded by a constant?

accepted.question_text: Why does avoiding the two rectangulation patterns shown in Figure 9 produce Catalan-number many rectangulations, and can one give a formal bijection explaining this enumeration?

evidence.quote: Question 1: The number of rectangulations that avoid the two patterns in Figure 9 simultaneously, produces the famous Catalan numbers (A000108). Is there an explanation for this phenomenon? Can we give a formal bijection?

accepted.question_text: Why does avoiding the three rectangulation patterns shown in Figure 10 produce Baxter-number many rectangulations, and can one give a formal bijection explaining this enumeration?

evidence.quote: Question 2: The number of rectangulations that avoid the three patterns in Figure 10 simultaneously produces the Baxter numbers (A001181). Can we give a formal bijection?

accepted.question_text: Is there a general bijection between rectangulations that avoid a rectangulation pattern P and permutations that avoid a corresponding mesh permutation pattern μ(P)?

evidence.quote: Question 3: Is there a general bijection between rectangulations avoiding a particular rectangulation pattern P and permutations avoiding a corresponding (mesh) permutation pattern μ(P)?

accepted.question_text: Is the wiggly flip graph WFG_n, whose vertices are wiggly pseudotriangulations and whose edges are flips between adjacent facets of the wiggly complex, Hamiltonian for every n?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 7. The wiggly flip graph is Hamiltonian.

accepted.question_text: For an arbitrary finite point set P in the plane equipped with the wiggly-arc construction defined in the booklet, is the reduced wiggly complex RWCP always the boundary complex of a simplicial polytope?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 9 ([1]). For any point set P in the plane, the wiggly complex RWCP is the boundary complex of a simplicial polytope.

accepted.question_text: For an arbitrary finite point set P in the plane equipped with the wiggly-arc construction defined in the booklet, is the wiggly flip graph WFG_P Hamiltonian?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 10. For any point set P in the plane, the wiggly flip graph WFGP is Hamiltonian.

accepted.question_text: Can the construction that realizes the aligned-point wiggly complex as the boundary of the wigglyhedron be adapted to give a more combinatorial construction of the polytope of pseudotriangulations that depends only on the order type, equivalently the oriented matroid, of the point configuration?

evidence.quote: 1. Can the construction of Theorem 6 be adapted to provide a more combinatorial construction of the polytope of pseudotriangulations [5], that would only depend on the order type (aka oriented matroid [2]) of the point configuration?

accepted.question_text: What is the dual interpretation of wiggly pseudotriangulations in terms of pseudoline arrangements, and can that interpretation be extended to other finite Coxeter groups?

evidence.quote: 2. What is the dual interpretation of wiggly pseudotriangulations as pseudoline arrangements? (see [4] for context) Can this interpretation be extended to other finite Coxeter groups? (see [3] for context).

accepted.question_text: What is the appropriate definition, structure, and theory of the multi wiggly complex?

evidence.quote: 3. What is the multi wiggly complex?

accepted.question_text: Construct a flip-Gray code for permutations of order n > 2 using only prefix reversals of sizes n−2, n−1, and n.

evidence.quote: Question 1: Big 3: Construct a flip-Gray code for permutations of order n > 2 where only flips of size n−2, n−1, and n are allowed.

accepted.question_text: Construct a flip-Gray code for signed permutations of order n, representing burnt pancakes, using only prefix reversals of sizes n−2, n−1, and n.

evidence.quote: Question 2: Big 3 (burnt): Construct a flip-Gray code for signed permutations (burnt pancakes) of order n where only flips of size n−2, n−1, and n are allowed.

accepted.question_text: Construct a flip-Gray code for permutations of order n using only prefix reversals of sizes 2, n−1, and n.

evidence.quote: Question 3: Construct a flip-Gray code for permutations of order n where only flips of size 2, n − 1, and n are allowed.

accepted.question_text: Let SP(n) be the shorthand permutations of order n and U*_n the lexicographically smallest universal cycle for SP(n). Is there an O(n)-time successor rule for generating successive symbols of U*_n, equivalently a simple parent rule for constructing a cycle-joining tree on the necklace representatives of SP(n)?

evidence.quote: Question 1: Is there a O(n)-time successor rule for determining successive symbols in U*n? This can be accomplished by finding a simple cycle-joining approach to construct U*n; in other words, is there a simple parent rule to construct a cycle-joining tree for necklace representatives of SP(n)?

accepted.question_text: What are the lexicographically smallest universal cycles U*_6 and U*_7 for shorthand permutations?

evidence.quote: Question 2: What is U*6 and U*7? Since U*6 has length 6! = 720, a brute force search already seems infeasible. However, it may be critical to answering the previous question.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a binary universal partial cycle for every length n = 2^j with j ≥ 2 in which wildcard symbols occur at every n-th position, and in particular can one construct such a cycle for n = 16?

evidence.quote: Question 1: Does there exist a (binary) UPC for all n = 2j, j ⩾ 2, where wildcards appear at every n-th position? As a starting point, can we construct a UPC for n = 24 = 16?

accepted.question_text: Let n = 2^j and let the co-necklace cycles of binary strings of length n be partitioned into two equally sized sets S1 = {α1, …, αm} and S2 = {β1, …, βm}. Can one always choose the partition so that each paired cycles α_i and β_i differ in exactly two positions that are n bits apart?

evidence.quote: Question 2: Let n = 2j. Define a partition of co-necklace cycles into two equal sized sets S1 = {α1, α2, . . . , αm} and S2 = {β1, β2, . . . , βm} such that αi and βi differ in exactly two positions n bits apart for each 1 ⩽ i ⩽ m.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a constant-amortized-time algorithm that lists one representative from each k-ary unlabeled necklace class of length n? The question is already open and interesting for fixed alphabets k = 3 and k = 4, and if k is not fixed then an O(n)-amortized algorithm would already be notable.

evidence.quote: Question: Does there exist a CAT algorithm to list representatives of each k-ary unlabeled necklace class of order n? Even the special cases fixing k = 3 and k = 4 are interesting. If k is not fixed, an O(n)-amortized time algorithm may be a nice result.

accepted.question_text: Have bifurcated ordered trees, whose children are ordered but each child is also designated as a left-child or right-child, already been studied in the literature or used in applications, and is there a natural bijection between these trees and other combinatorial objects counted by OEIS sequence A006013?

evidence.quote: Question 1: Have BOTs been previously studied or applied in previous academic investigations? Is there a natural bijection between BOTs and objects with the same enumeration sequences as detailed in sequence A006013 [1]?

accepted.question_text: Is there a simple and efficient Gray-code algorithm to generate all bifurcated ordered trees of order n, and can the resulting ordering be ranked and unranked efficiently?

evidence.quote: Question 2: Is there a simple and efficient (Gray code) algorithm to generate all BOTs of order n? Can the resulting ordering be efficiently ranked/unranked?

accepted.question_text: Can one construct pivot Gray codes for spanning trees of broader classes of planar or other graphs, where consecutive spanning trees differ by exchanging two edges incident to the same vertex, and can such constructions be turned into efficient algorithms? What happens if the exchange condition is weakened so that the two exchanged edges need only be incident to the same face?
accepted.context_brief: Pivot Gray codes for spanning trees

evidence.quote: Question: Can we derive pivot Gray codes for listing the spanning trees of more general classes of (planar) graphs? If so, do these constructions translate into efficient algorithms? What about another closeness condition for plane graphs, namely “e and f are incident to the same face, but not necessarily to the same vertex” (this is a pivot exchange in the dual spanning tree)?

accepted.question_text: For a set S of n = 2m points in the plane in general position, is the flip graph of all plane perfect matchings on S connected using only flips that change at most k edges for some fixed constant k, or at least for some sublinear k?
accepted.context_brief: Connectivity of plane perfect matching flip graph

evidence.quote: Question 1: For a given set S with n = 2m points is the flip-graph of all plane perfect matchings on S connected via ≤ k-flips for some constant or at least sublinear k?

accepted.question_text: What is the smallest value of k such that every plane perfect matching always admits at least one k-flip?
accepted.context_brief: Shortest always-available flip in plane matchings

evidence.quote: Question 2: How long is the shortest k-flip that can always be made in a plane perfect matching?

accepted.question_text: If one generalizes the flip operation on plane perfect matchings by allowing the alternating cycle underlying a k-flip, for k ≥ 3, to have crossings among its own edges while the two participating matchings remain plane and no other edges are crossed, how does this affect the connectivity and shortest-flip questions above?

evidence.quote: Question 3: If for a k-flip, k ⩾ 3, we allow crossings between the different edges of the alternating cycle (but not with other edges), how does this influence the answers to the previous two questions?

accepted.question_text: For token graphs T(G, a⃗) with a fixed number k of colors, what is the computational complexity of deciding whether the token graph is Hamiltonian, especially for intermediate values 3 ≤ k ≤ n−1?

evidence.quote: Question 1: How hard is to decide wether a token graph with (fixed) k colors is Hamiltonian? It is in P for k = 1 (trivially) and k = n (by Tchuente’s result). On the other hand it is NP-complete for k = 2 (as T(G,(1, n − 1)) =∼ G). What can we say for k = 3, . . . , n − 1?

accepted.question_text: Is there a structural characterization of when token graphs are Hamiltonian when the underlying graph G is restricted to be a tree, a path, or a cycle?
accepted.context_brief: Hamiltonicity of token graphs on special graphs

evidence.quote: Question 2: Is there a characterization for Hamiltonicity of Token graphs (similar to Tchuente’s result for n colors) when the graphs are trees/paths/cycles?

accepted.question_text: Can the token swapping problem on a connected graph G with a given token permutation π be solved in singly exponential time 2^{O(n)}?

evidence.quote: Question: Can the token swapping problem be solved in singly exponential time?

accepted.question_text: When the base graph X in the friends-and-strangers graph FS(X, Y) is a tree, what can be said about the connected components of FS(X, Y), and is there a natural correspondence between those connected components and some other interesting combinatorial structures?

evidence.quote: Question 1: When X is a tree, what can we say about the connected components of FS(X, Y)? Is there a (natural) correspondence between the connected components and another (interesting) combinatorial structures?

accepted.question_text: For the local connectedness problem in friends-and-strangers graphs, where one is given two bijections σ and σ′ and asked whether they lie in the same connected component of FS(X, Y), does PSPACE-hardness persist when the base graph X is restricted to be a tree?
accepted.context_brief: Local connectedness for tree-based FS graphs

evidence.quote: Question 2: Is the local connectedness problem still hard (e.g. PSPACE-complete) even when X is constrained to be trees?

accepted.question_text: Can every matching of the d-dimensional hypercube Q_d, for d ≥ 2, be extended to a Hamilton cycle?

evidence.quote: Question 1: Can every matching of Qd, d ⩾ 2, be extended to a Hamilton cycle?

accepted.question_text: Given a matching M of Q_d or K(Q_d), can one characterize which cycle lengths ℓ admit a cycle C of length ℓ extending M, or at least prove useful upper bounds of the form |C| ≤ f(|M|) for an extending cycle whose length depends reasonably on the size of M?

evidence.quote: Question 2: Can we instead prove a theorem about a cycle C extending a given matching M, such that the length of C is relatively short compared to the size of M, i.e., such that |C| ⩽ f(|M|) for some reasonable function f? Obviously, we will always have |C| ⩾ 2|M|. More generally, given a matching M of Qd or K(Qd), for which integers ℓ is there a cycle C with |C| = ℓ that extends M?

accepted.question_text: Is there a matching in K(Q_d) or in the complete bipartite graph B(Q_d) on the hypercube vertices that can be extended to a cycle factor but cannot be extended to a Hamilton cycle?

evidence.quote: Question 3: Is there a matching of K(Qd) or B(Qd) that is extendable to a cycle factor but not to a Hamilton cycle?

accepted.question_text: Which matchings of Q_d or K(Q_d) can be extended to Hamilton paths with prescribed endpoints?
accepted.context_brief: Hypercube matchings and prescribed-end Hamilton paths

evidence.quote: Question 4: Which matchings of Qd or K(Qd) can be extended to Hamilton paths with prescribed ends?

accepted.question_text: For the path graph P_n and a chosen target vertex i, what is the exact minimum stacking weight μ(P_n, i), where each move transfers an entire stack of k cups along a graph distance of exactly k?

evidence.quote: Question 1: What is the value of μ(Pn, i) for a path Pn, n ⩾ 1, and vertex i ∈ [n]?

accepted.question_text: Given a Hamilton path P in a graph and a target vertex t on that path, which strategy of stacking cups along P achieves the minimum possible total stacking weight?
accepted.context_brief: Optimal stacking strategy along a Hamilton path

evidence.quote: Question 2: Given a Hamilton path P in a graph, which strategy of stacking along the path P to a target t has smallest weight?

accepted.question_text: Given a traceable graph G, which Hamilton path in G permits a cup-stacking strategy of minimum total weight?
accepted.context_brief: Best Hamilton path for cup stacking

evidence.quote: Question 3: Given a traceable graph G, which Hamilton path in G allows a stacking strategy of smallest weight?
